steps.body:
Every lesson so far has ASSUMED that f′ > 0 means the curve rises. Nobody proved it. The MVT does.

Take any x₁ < x₂. The MVT gives a c with f(x₂) − f(x₁) = f′(c)(x₂ − x₁). If f′ is positive everywhere, the right-hand side is positive — so f(x₂) > f(x₁).

**f′ > 0 ⇒ increasing.** Not a picture. A proof.

explanationVariants: If f′ = 0 everywhere, the MVT gives f(x₂) − f(x₁) = 0·(x₂ − x₁) = 0 for ANY two points. So f takes the same value everywhere: it is constant.
This is what makes the + C legitimate: two functions with the same derivative differ by a constant, because their difference has zero derivative.

widget.prompt: On an interval, f′(x) = 0 for every x. What follows?

options.label: f is constant
options.feedback: Right, and this is what finally JUSTIFIES the + C: if F′ = G′ then (F − G)′ = 0, so F − G is constant.

options.label: f is identically zero
options.feedback: f(x) = 7 has zero derivative and is nowhere near zero. Zero SLOPE, not zero value.

options.label: f increases slowly
options.feedback: Not at all — it does not increase. The MVT shows f(x₂) equals f(x₁) exactly, for every pair.

options.label: No conclusion follows
options.feedback: The MVT needs nothing more. Two points and a zero derivative are enough to force equality.

steps.body: The debt calculus has been carrying.

widget.prompt: Three facts you have been using on credit.

panels.title: f′ > 0 means rising
panels.body: Used in every sign chart, in the first-derivative test, in every optimisation. It LOOKS obvious. But 'the tangent points up here' and 'the curve is higher over there' are different claims, and only the MVT connects them.

panels.title: f′ = 0 everywhere means constant
panels.body: Used silently every time you wrote + C. Two antiderivatives of the same f differ by a constant precisely BECAUSE their difference has zero derivative — and only the MVT says that forces constancy.

panels.title: So the MVT is load-bearing
panels.body: It looks like a curiosity about parallel lines. It is actually the beam holding up the first-derivative test, the sign charts, and the whole theory of antiderivatives.

widget.continueFeedback: Keep going — the third panel is why the theorem has a name.
widget.successFeedback: The MVT is not a curiosity. It is the proof underneath the machinery you have been using all course.

steps.body: Bound a function you cannot see.
explanationVariants: MVT: f(5) − f(1) = f′(c)·4 for some c. If f′ ≤ 3 everywhere, then f(5) − f(1) ≤ 12, so f(5) ≤ 2 + 12 = 14.
You never learn what f is. The derivative's bound becomes a bound on the function.

widget.prompt: f(1) = 2 and f′(x) ≤ 3 for all x. What is the largest possible value of f(5)?

commonErrors.feedback: That is the bound on the DERIVATIVE. Over 4 units of x, f can gain at most 3 × 4 = 12, so f(5) ≤ 2 + 12 = 14.
That is the maximum GAIN. Add the starting value: f(5) ≤ 2 + 12 = 14.
Check the width: from x = 1 to x = 5 is 4 units, not 5. So the gain is at most 12.

steps.body:
And it settles the last loose end from C4.

If F′ = G′ everywhere, then (F − G)′ = 0, so **F − G is constant**. That is *why* every antiderivative of f has the form F + C, and why the + C is a complete description of the family rather than a hedge.

The theorem you almost skipped is the one holding up the integral.
Why + C is the whole family.
explanationVariants: If F and G both have derivative f, then (F − G)′ = f − f = 0, so F − G is constant by the MVT. Hence G = F + C, and there are no other antiderivatives.
Without the MVT you could not rule out some exotic antiderivative that differs from F by something other than a constant.

widget.prompt: Why do all antiderivatives of f on an interval differ only by a constant?

options.label: The MVT makes their difference constant
options.feedback: Right. Without the MVT you could not rule out some stranger relationship, and the + C would be a hope rather than a theorem.

options.label: The definition alone proves the + C form
options.feedback: The definition says F′ = f. It does not, by itself, say that ALL such F differ by a constant — that is a theorem, and the MVT proves it.

options.label: Constants have zero derivative
options.feedback: That shows F + C IS an antiderivative. The harder direction — that there are no OTHERS — is what needs the MVT.

options.label: The + C form is an assumption
options.feedback: It is proved, not assumed. That is the difference the MVT makes.

hints: Use the MVT on [0, 3]: f(3) − f(0) = f′(c)·3 for some c.
You are told 2 ≤ f′ ≤ 4, so the gain is between 2×3 = 6 and 4×3 = 12.
f(0) = 1, so f(3) is between 7 and 13. The question asks for the SMALLEST possible value.
explanationVariants: The minimum gain is 2 × 3 = 6, so the smallest possible f(3) is 1 + 6 = 7.
The MVT turns a bound on the derivative into a bound on the function — in both directions at once.

widget.prompt: f(0) = 1 and 2 ≤ f′(x) ≤ 4 everywhere. What is the SMALLEST possible value of f(3)?

commonErrors.feedback: That is the LARGEST possible value (gain of 4 × 3 = 12). The smallest uses the slowest allowed growth: 2 × 3 = 6, giving 7.
That is the minimum GAIN. Add the starting value f(0) = 1 to get 7.
That is the lower bound on the derivative. Multiply by the width 3 and add f(0) = 1.

takeaways: f′ > 0 ⇒ increasing, and f′ = 0 everywhere ⇒ constant. Both are PROVED by the MVT, not assumed.
That second fact is why + C describes the whole family of antiderivatives, with no exceptions.
A bound on f′ becomes a bound on f — you can constrain a function you have never seen.
steps.teaser: Next chapter: put every chart together and draw the curve.

concept.body: The MVT converts a fact about the DERIVATIVE into a fact about the FUNCTION. If the slope is always positive, the function must rise. If the slope is always zero, it cannot move at all. If the slope is bounded, the function's growth is bounded too.

explanationVariants: f′ = 0 everywhere means f cannot change, so f(10) = f(0) = 5.

widget.prompt: f′(x) = 0 for all x, and f(0) = 5. Find f(10).

commonErrors.feedback: That is the DERIVATIVE. The function itself is stuck at its starting value of 5.
That is x. A zero derivative means f never moves: f(10) = f(0) = 5.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Zero derivative everywhere ⇒ f is constant ⇒ f(10) = 5.
